title: Mastery challenge: two resistors in parallel

questions.prompt: What must the interval you return guarantee?

choices.text: It holds every value the pair can take
choices.why: That is what an interval answer means, and the task adds that it should hold little else.

choices.text: Its centre is the nominal resistance
choices.why: The centre of the true range is not the value computed from the two nominal resistances.

choices.text: It is as narrow as the narrower input
choices.why: Nothing ties the width of the result to the width of one input.

questions.prompt: What does each interval produced along the way contain?

choices.why: A single value would throw the tolerance away.

choices.text: Every value that sub-expression can take
choices.why: Each supplied operation promises this for its inputs, so it holds step by step up to the final answer.

choices.text: The values of the step before it
choices.why: Each step computes a different quantity, in different units.

questions.prompt: How many times should each resistor's interval enter the arithmetic?

choices.why: Every further appearance is treated as a separate quantity free to take any value in the interval, which widens the result.
The second appearance is treated as a second, independent resistor.
The starter and a correct answer use the same operations and differ only in this.

questions.prompt: For 6.8 ± 10% and 4.7 ± 5% the starter returns about 2.20 to 3.49 ohms. The pair's real range is about 2.58 to 2.97. Where does the extra width come from?

choices.why: Division by an interval that excludes zero is sound; a correct answer here divides too.
The percentages are converted to plain bounds before any arithmetic happens.

choices.text: R1 taken as 6.12 and 7.48 at once
choices.why: The lower bound 2.20 is the smallest product, 6.12 × 4.465, over the largest sum, 7.48 + 4.935. No single resistor is at both ends.

checklist.step: Contain every possible resistance, however intervals are stored
Stay within 1% of the true range, and draw it

hints: Ask what the circuit can really do. Can one resistor be at its lowest and its highest value at the same moment?
Count how many times each resistor appears in the formula the starter evaluates, and what interval arithmetic assumes about each appearance.
Look for an algebraically equal way to write the combined resistance in which R1 and R2 each appear once.
